english: Connection of these automorphic functions with the higher continued-fraction algorithms.
topic: Hilbert sketches building a fundamental domain (Urbereich) for a substitution group by expanding convex bodies until they touch and fill space, proposes using it for automorphic functions linked to higher continued-fraction algorithms, and begins the case n=2 with lattice conditions for a reduced region.

triage.modern_statement: This is a programme question, not a precise theorem. Take a discrete group of substitutions (for n=2, essentially SL(2,Z) or GL(2,Z); in general SL(n,Z) acting on a space of lattices or quadratic forms). Build a fundamental domain for it by a Dirichlet/Voronoi-type method: grow convex bodies until they touch and fill space. Use that domain to define automorphic functions. Then ask how the domain and those functions relate to higher-dimensional continued-fraction algorithms such as Jacobi–Perron. The aim would be to generalise the classical link between the modular group's fundamental domain and ordinary continued fractions to dimension n>2. In modern terms: how do reduction theory and fundamental domains of SL(n,Z) relate to multidimensional continued fractions?
triage.answered_by: No one answered Hilbert's note directly, and I found no source that mentions it. Two later bodies of work cover parts of the idea. First, reduction theory and fundamental domains for arithmetic equivalence: Minkowski, 'Diskontinuitätsbereich für arithmetische Äquivalenz', J. reine angew. Math. 129 (1905). Second, the link between multidimensional continued fractions and the homogeneous space SL(n,Z)\SL(n,R): Lagarias, 'Geodesic multidimensional continued fractions' (1994), developed further by Khanin, Lopes Dias and Marklof (Comm. Math. Phys., 2006/07). The part about automorphic functions does not seem to have been carried out in that form.

evidence.claim: Minkowski's 1905 Crelle paper 'Diskontinuitätsbereich für arithmetische Äquivalenz' built the fundamental (reduction) domain for arithmetic equivalence of quadratic forms in n variables.

Lagarias (1994), 'Geodesic multidimensional continued fractions', introduced continued-fraction expansions built from Minkowski reduction theory and geodesic flow, so multidimensional continued fractions are tied to fundamental domains of SL(n,Z).

Khanin, Lopes Dias and Marklof build multidimensional continued fractions from the geodesic flow on Γ\G with G=SL(d,R) and Γ=SL(d,Z), which is identified with the space of lattices. They name Lagarias's ideas as the starting point and use a fundamental domain.

Lagarias's specific algorithm is said to be 'not really practical' because no efficient algorithm is known for the reduction step. So the link between reduction theory and multidimensional continued fractions is still being worked on.

triage.why: Hilbert's note asks an open-ended question about a connection; there is no specific conjecture to settle, and it is not one of his published problems. The fundamental-domain half was worked out by Minkowski (1905). The link between fundamental domains of SL(n,Z) and multidimensional continued fractions was set up much later by Lagarias (1994) and others, and research on it continues. I found no source that defines automorphic functions on such a domain and connects them to Jacobi–Perron-type algorithms, and nothing that cites Hilbert's diary. So the best label is a broadly known area that is still open and active, not a solved problem. The verdict is uncertain because the question is so loosely stated.
